e.t: This noun means “want of rain; drought”—a condition in which rain is absent or insufficient. It refers to dry conditions rather than to a person’s desire or need. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Jeremiah and once in Sirach. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the lack of rainfall, while the surrounding verse determines how that drought functions in its particular passage.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “sanctuary,” referring to a place set apart for God and worship. It commonly identifies the holy place connected with God’s presence, consecrated service, and the worship of his people. The word occurs 59 times in the Greek Old Testament, including the Deuterocanonical books, so it represents a recurring scriptural term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a place made holy and devoted to God.

Adraazar is a personal name, rendered “Adraazar” or “Athraazar.” It identifies a specific person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs 21 times, appearing in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. The precise person being identified depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a proper name.

Azaki is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:17, and is rendered as “Azaki.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is chiefly identifying: it distinguishes one person from others in the genealogical record. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific family connection or role.

This adverb means “according to” or “accordingly,” indicating that something is done or stated in keeping with what has already been said or with an established measure or direction. It describes how an action or statement corresponds to something else, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:23; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “hear”: to perceive or receive what is spoken or sounded. It is a common action word, used 972 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning concerns hearing, while the surrounding passage determines whether the word refers to hearing a person, a report, a cry, or another sound. The English rendering “hear” is also directly attested in the translation evidence, supporting this straightforward sense.

This noun refers to a hearer—someone who listens—or an auditor, a person receiving what is spoken or taught. It presents the listener as the one who attends to words, rather than the one who delivers them. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah 3:3 and once in Sirach 3:29. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “of the sea,” describing something connected with or belonging to the sea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs three times, in two verses: twice in Job and once in Jeremiah. As an adjective, it modifies a noun, identifying a sea-related quality or association. Its basic meaning remains concise and specific; the surrounding verse determines what sea-related thing is being described.

gl: raise by a lever; force open
d: raise by a lever; force open

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to raise something by using a lever or to force it open. It describes a deliberate physical action in which leverage is used to lift, pry, or open something that resists. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 10:5. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the use of leverage to raise or open.

This verb means to “show off” or “demonstrate”—to make something visible or plainly known. It can describe displaying a person, thing, quality, or achievement so that others recognize it. As an action word, it focuses on presenting or making something evident rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books.

This Greek LXX noun means an error: something done or judged wrongly. It refers to a mistake or wrong act, naming the fault itself rather than describing a person who commits it. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, both in Judges 20, at Judges 20:6 and 20:10. Its exact force in either verse is best understood from the surrounding sentence and passage.

Arme is a proper name, preserved as “Arme,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:33. The available information identifies it as a specific name but does not establish from the name alone whether it refers to a person, settlement, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “illness” or “sickness”—a condition of physical unhealth. It names the state of being sick rather than an action or person. In the Greek text of Sirach, it occurs five times, including one rendering as “sickness.” The surrounding passage determines whether the word refers generally to bodily weakness or to a particular health condition, but its central meaning remains a state of illness.

This noun means “one who practises any art”—a person who develops and exercises skill in an art or skilled practice. It identifies the practitioner rather than the art itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 12:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person engaged in practising an art or skill.

This Greek LXX verb means “flash”—to shine suddenly or give a brief burst of light. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or lasting condition. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Psalms and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the central idea remains sudden, vivid shining. The word is found at Psalms 143:6 and Wisdom 11:18.

This Greek LXX verb means “dismiss; leave”: it describes sending someone away, letting someone go, or departing from something. Its basic sense can apply to a person being released, a matter being allowed to pass, or someone leaving a place. It occurs 102 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is a broad, commonly used action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any verse depends on what or whom the sentence says is being left or dismissed.

Achian, also given as “Akhian,” is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Samuel 23:33. Because it is a personal name, its ordinary meaning is the individual it identifies; the name itself does not provide a broader definition without additional context or a related explanation. The passage reference establishes its occurrence, but the verse text is needed to explain the person’s role there.

Belsattim is a proper name, also given as “Velsattim.” It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 33:49. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here; the lexical information establishes the name itself and its alternate English form.

This noun means “pasturage” or “pasture”—land or vegetation where animals feed. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe the plant growth produced from the earth and the grassy provision affected by hail or locusts. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, with its earliest occurrences in Genesis and its latest in Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage focuses on the land, the plants growing there, or food available for animals.

This verb means “stuff,” describing the action of putting something into another thing. It refers to an action, not a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 57:5. Its basic lexical sense is clear, but the verse text is not available here, so the precise object and force of the action cannot be explained. The word’s ordinary meaning remains the act of stuffing something.

Giōn is a proper name identifying a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered Gion and functions as a designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or general object. The name appears five times, in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its exact reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself is simply a name used to identify something known in the biblical account.

This Greek LXX noun means “loan”: money or property given to someone with the expectation that it will be repaid. It names the thing borrowed rather than the act of lending or repaying. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical Greek text, including three occurrences in Deuteronomy and one in 4 Maccabees. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and teaching. (Deuteronomy 15:8, 15:10; 24:11; 4 Maccabees 2:8.)

This Greek LXX verb means “cowardly.” It describes acting without courage, especially when facing something difficult or threatening. The word functions as an action word, focusing on how someone responds rather than simply labeling a person’s character. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX material, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Greek LXX noun means “diadem,” a distinctive crown or head ornament associated with honor, rank, or royalty. It names the object itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, including passages in Esther, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 1 Maccabees. Its use can refer to royal adornment or a symbolic crown, but the exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “narration” or “narrative”: a telling or account of events, words, or matters. As a noun, it refers to the account itself rather than to the act of speaking. It occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Judges, Habakkuk, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on what is being recounted and how the surrounding sentence presents that account.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “imagine” or “seem.” It describes what a person thinks or supposes, or how something appears to be the case. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis falls on someone’s impression or on the apparent nature of a matter. It occurs 53 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including the deuterocanonical books, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than for one narrow situation.

This verb means to “give allegiance” or be “subject,” describing the act of placing oneself under another’s authority or serving under that authority. It can refer to human service, political submission, or devoted obedience, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical books, it occurs 140 times, showing that submission and service are recurring ideas in this corpus. Its precise emphasis—whether loyal service or compelled subjection—must be determined from the immediate context.

This adjective means “stone-deaf,” describing someone who is unable to hear. It presents deafness as severe or complete, using “stone” to emphasize the condition’s hardness and lack of response to sound. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 4:11. The word itself identifies a physical hearing condition; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise significance there.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an idol’s temple—the place associated with an idol’s worship. Its basic meaning is a temple connected with an idol, rather than a general temple without that association. The word occurs three times in the deuterocanonical portion of the Greek LXX, in 1 Maccabees and Bel and the Dragon. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This adjective describes someone or something as peaceful—marked by peace rather than conflict. It can identify people, conditions, or actions that promote calm and friendly relations. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 47 times, so its basic sense is used across various situations rather than being limited to one setting. The word’s exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains peacefulness and the absence or resolution of hostility.

Eleketh is a proper name—a personal or place name preserved as “Eleketh.” It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, so its significance comes from the person or place identified by the surrounding passage rather than from a broader definition. In the Greek LXX, Eleketh occurs once, in Joshua 19:25. The reference identifies where the name appears, but the specific person or location it denotes must be determined from the verse and its surrounding context.

Eliazai is a proper personal name, also rendered Eliaze. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 12:6. The name itself does not provide a general concept or instruction; its role is to identify the individual named in that passage. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific place in the account.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “business,” referring to commercial activity or trade. It points to the activity or sphere of doing business, not to an individual merchant or a specific object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs two times, in Isaiah 23:17 and Ezekiel 27:3. Its basic sense is the general activity of conducting business, while its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “atone for” or “appease.” It describes an action intended to address offense or guilt and restore favor. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in passages concerning sacrificial or priestly service, while also appearing in other settings. The word occurs 105 times in the LXX corpus, across 97 verses, so its precise expression depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains making atonement or seeking reconciliation through an intentional act.

This Greek LXX verb means “hear from”: receiving communication, an answer, or a response from someone. It describes hearing as something that comes from a person or source, rather than merely noticing a sound. The word appears 95 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so it is a recurring verb for receiving such communication. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “intermarriage,” referring to marriage between people from different peoples or communities. It is a noun naming that kind of union rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 23:12. The precise concern expressed in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider setting, but the word itself identifies the joining of different peoples through marriage. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific: intermarriage as a recognized relationship between distinct groups.

This noun means a letter: a written message or document sent from one person or group to another. It can refer to a single letter or to letters collectively, as shown by its use in both singular and plural translations. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 55 times across 53 verses, especially in books that recount official communication, royal decisions, or correspondence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “follow” or “obey.” It describes moving after someone, staying with a person, or responding to a direction with compliance. The word can therefore express either physical following or submission to guidance, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

Esthamō is a proper name, rendered as “Esthamo.” It identifies a person or place named Esthamo rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:42. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s particular identity and role must be understood from that passage itself. The word’s basic meaning is therefore its function as the name Esthamo in the Greek Old Testament.

Esōth, also written Esoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded meaning is simply the personal or place name “Esōth; Esoth,” so it identifies someone or something named Esoth. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:10. The name itself does not provide further meaning without the surrounding verse and passage.

This adverb means “intensely,” describing an action carried out with great force or strong effort. It adds emphasis to the action or manner being expressed, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 6:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is concentrated strength or earnest intensity.

Zathoes is a proper name identifying a person; the name is also given as Zathis. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it appears once, in Ezra 8:5. Since this is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, it does not itself express an action, quality, or idea. Its precise role in Ezra 8:5 depends on the surrounding passage, but the name’s lexical sense is simply the person it identifies.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Ēserai” or “Isere.” It is not a general description, action, or spiritual quality, but an identifying personal name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:37. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic lexical function is to identify an individual.

This word is a proper name, identifying Ēcha, also given as Ikha. It is not a general description, action, or quality, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 6:28. Since no verse text or wider context is provided here, its specific identity in that passage cannot be explained further from the name alone.

This word means a band: a group of people gathered together. As a noun, it identifies the group itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Jeremiah and once in Wisdom. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what kind of band is meant in either passage, but the word’s basic sense is a gathered company or group.

This verb means “burn incense,” referring to the act of burning fragrant material in worship. It describes an action rather than the incense itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 27 times, showing repeated use for this kind of ritual service. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the act of burning incense before God or in connection with worship.

gl: part behind the thigh and knee; ham
d: part behind the thigh and knee; ham

e.t: This noun refers to the part behind the thigh and knee, commonly called the ham. It names a specific area of the leg rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 18:21. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself has a straightforward bodily meaning: the flesh or joint located behind the knee and at the lower back of the thigh.

This interjection means “see!” or “here I am.” It draws attention to something being presented, noticed, or announced, and it can also express a person’s immediate response when making himself or herself present. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 1,067 times, so it is a broadly used attention-getting expression rather than a rare technical term. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what follows it and the surrounding context.

This word means “sacred.” It describes something regarded as holy, especially in relation to worship, holy places, or things devoted to God. It can function as an adjective describing what is sacred or as a noun referring to something sacred. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, with most occurrences in the books of the Maccabees. Its precise force in a passage depends on what sacred thing is being described.

Iephies, also rendered Iefies, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 5:15. Because the available information provides the name and reference but not the verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further here.

This Greek LXX verb means “fatigued,” describing someone who has become weary or exhausted. It focuses on a state of diminished strength rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing in Job, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains becoming worn down or tired.

This verb means to crush something into pieces or break it apart. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes forceful destruction rather than a gentle separation or ordinary movement. Its two occurrences appear in Psalms and Isaiah, showing that it is a specific action word for breaking something decisively. The exact object and force intended in either passage are understood from the surrounding verse.

This Greek LXX verb means “dwell”: to remain or stay in a place. It describes continued residence or staying rather than a brief visit. In the Septuagint Old Testament, it occurs five times, from Genesis through Joshua, showing this basic sense across several books. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself points to remaining somewhere. It is an action word describing where someone stays.

This noun refers to “falling down” or a “gap”—either the act of coming down or an opening left where something is absent. Its basic sense points to a downward fall or a break in continuity, rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Psalm 143:14; the surrounding verse text is needed to determine which aspect the context emphasizes.

This Greek word means “put down” or “lay down.” It is a verb describing the act of placing something in a lower position or setting it down. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from 1 Chronicles, Esther, Psalms, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on what is being placed and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to “hit exactly”—to strike a person or target with precise aim. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs only once, at 2 Maccabees 14:43. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a direct, accurate strike.

This word means “kernel,” referring to the small inner part of a seed or grain. It is a noun used for the seed’s essential interior rather than for the whole plant or crop. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Lamentations and once in Sirach. The exact significance of the kernel in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its imagery.

This Greek LXX noun means “ring,” referring to a circular object. It is used for physical rings associated with tabernacle furnishings and their construction, especially in Exodus. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across nine verses, with most occurrences in Exodus. Its basic sense remains simple and concrete: a ring or circular fitting used as part of an object or structure.

This noun describes someone or something endowed with speech—that is, given the ability to speak. It points to the possession or exercise of speech rather than merely being present or silent. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Job 38:14, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated appearances. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: having speech or being capable of speaking.

This word means “basin,” referring to a container used to hold water, especially in a washing context. It is a noun, so it identifies the vessel itself rather than the action of washing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Sirach and twice in Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

Mageddōn, also rendered Mayeththon, is a proper name identifying a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 9:27. The name itself supplies the identification, while the surrounding verse is needed to understand what happened there. This word should therefore be read as a geographical name preserved in the biblical account, not as a general term with a broader everyday meaning.

This noun means “diviner,” referring to a person identified by the practice or role of divination. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, each in a different verse, from Joshua through Zechariah. The word therefore names a kind of person rather than an action or object. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “about to” or “impending,” describing something expected to happen soon or that is on the point of occurring. It can point to an approaching action, event, or condition, rather than merely something possible or distant. The word appears 42 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, so it serves as a recurring way to express nearness in time. Its exact force in any verse depends on what event or action the surrounding sentence identifies as impending.

This Greek LXX noun means “length,” referring to the measurement of something from one end to the other. It is used for the dimensions of objects and structures, including the ark, the tabernacle furnishings, and temple areas. The word occurs 83 times in the Greek Old Testament, showing a regular practical use in descriptions of size and construction. Its basic sense remains the measured extent of something along its longest dimension.

This adjective means “hateful”: it describes someone or something viewed with hatred or strong aversion. It identifies a hated quality or condition rather than expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, it occurs nine times, appearing in Genesis, Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what person or thing is being described there.

Mollath is a proper name, functioning as the personal name of an individual rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the LXX text, in 2 Chronicles 11:18. The available lexical information gives the name as “Mollath,” but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of the name itself. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

This LXX Greek word means “musician,” referring to a person identified by involvement with music. Used as a noun, it names such a person rather than an action or abstract quality. It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus represented here, including passages in Genesis, Ezekiel, Daniel, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. The central meaning remains focused and concrete: a musician. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This proper noun identifies a person as a “Nelamitēs” or “Nelamitis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a general description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Jeremiah 36:24 and Jeremiah 36:31. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated confidently, while the person’s particular role in each passage must be understood from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means “depart”—to go away or leave. It describes the act of moving away from a place or situation, rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material represented here, including five occurrences in Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains departure: someone or something goes away. This is a normal action word, expressing leaving or removal from where one was present.

This Greek LXX verb means “collect weapons.” It describes the act of gathering weapons together, whether for preparation, organization, or use; the word itself focuses on collecting rather than explaining the larger purpose. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both in 2 Maccabees 8, so its ordinary sense is clear, while its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding passage. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This adverb means “all over” or “from every side.” It describes something that comes, spreads, surrounds, or is present in every direction rather than from only one place. The central idea is complete surrounding or coverage. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, showing a repeated directional sense across different passages. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what is being described, but the word itself points broadly in every direction.

This Greek LXX verb means to walk around or along. It describes the physical act of moving on foot, whether someone is walking through a place, beside something, or from one location to another. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its normal sense is straightforward and practical rather than limited to a special religious use. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “bitterly,” describing how something is done with bitterness, intense grief, or harsh feeling. It modifies an action rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the action and surrounding words, but its central idea remains an intensely painful, distressed, or harsh manner of acting.

This noun means “usury” or “unjust gains”—wrongful profit taken from another, especially through lending. It refers to an added financial gain regarded as unjust rather than to ordinary, fair repayment. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs six times, including four occurrences in Ezekiel, where it is associated with conduct condemned as unjust. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means to carry something through by “bringing it about” or “furnishing” what is needed. It describes an action that provides, supplies, or produces a result. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 15:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense is active provision or accomplishment rather than a merely passive possession.

This verb means to “fight in front,” describing someone who takes the forward position in a struggle or battle. It presents active participation rather than merely watching or supporting from behind. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 18:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: standing at the front and engaging in the fight on behalf of others or alongside them.

This verb means to “fill up toward” something or to “replenish” what is lacking. It describes an action that brings something to greater fullness or restores its supply. As a verb, it focuses on the act of filling or making up what is needed, rather than naming the thing being filled. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 19:4; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

This LXX noun refers to what is foremost—the first or leading position. It identifies something placed at the front or given priority rather than something secondary. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, once in 1 Kings 10:19 and once in 2 Maccabees 15:35. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is what stands first or foremost.

This word means “frost” or “cold,” referring to a chill or freezing condition. It is a noun, so it names the condition itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy 28:22 and Daniel 3:67. Its use belongs to the ordinary language of severe or penetrating cold, while the surrounding passage determines the particular force of the reference.

Salamia is a proper name identifying a specific person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, not a descriptive word to be translated into an ordinary concept. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:14. The surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly whom or what Salamia identifies there.

This word means “lizard,” referring to a small crawling reptile. It is a noun used to name the creature itself, rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Leviticus 11:30. The precise significance of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a lizard. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s wording, without merging it with a separate Hebrew or Greek New Testament word.

Setirōtha, also rendered Setirotha, is a proper name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 3:26. The available lexical information preserves the name itself rather than giving an additional descriptive meaning, so it should be read as a name, not translated as an ordinary action, quality, or object. Its precise reference in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and verse text; the word-level information identifies only its naming function.
